title: Conflict settings: risks, safety, prolonged care
text:
54
|

 
Conflict 
Situational context 
Armed conflict creates some of the most complex and dangerous conditions in which first aid is 
delivered. Today, conflicts increasingly take place in urban and peri-urban environments, where 
civilians, responders and infrastructure are exposed to violence. At the same time, many conflicts 
extend into remote, frontier and isolated areas, where access to services is limited and 
evacuation to advanced care may take hours or days. Unlike sudden-onset disasters or 
time-limited epidemics, armed conflict is characterized by intentional violence and sustained 
insecurity, requiring first aid providers to operate under continuous and unpredictable threat. 
In conflict-affected settings, first aid is not only a health intervention but a life-preserving 
humanitarian act, often delivered under direct threat. Responders must balance the urgency of 
life-saving care with continuous assessment of security risks. The ability to adapt care, education, 
and decision-making to rapidly changing conditions is essential. 
For the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, first aid in conflict is grounded in 
humanitarian principles and closely linked to broader efforts to protect civilians, ensure access to 
care and support community resilience. 
Characteristics of conflict-affected settings 
Conflict settings are defined by persistent insecurity, damaged infrastructure and disrupted 
health systems. Weapons, tactics and environment shape injury patterns, while access to 
advanced care is often limited by insecurity, checkpoints or destroyed facilities. 
Unlike disaster or epidemic contexts, the threat is often intentional and ongoing. Responders 
may face direct targeting, secondary attacks or restrictions on movement. This reality profoundly 
shapes how first aid is provided and taught. Understanding how conflict manifests across the 
remote–urban continuum is essential for adapting first aid systems, training approaches and 
expectations of care. 
Conflict affects settings differently along the remote-urban continuum: 
-  Urban conflict often involves blast injuries, wound trauma, structural collapse and mass 
casualty incidents in densely populated areas. 
-  Rural and remote areas may see fewer casualties overall, but longer evacuation times 
and limited stabilization capacity. 
-  Deep remote and isolated areas frequently rely on community members as the sole 
providers of initial care, with longer delays to advanced care. 
Across all settings, civilians—including children, older adults and persons with disabilities—bear 
a growing share of the burden of injury and death (ICRC, 2016). 

|
55 

 
Health risks and injury patterns 
The dominant health risks in conflict settings are traumatic injuries, particularly those associated 
with weapons and explosive devices. Uncontrolled bleeding is widely recognized as the leading 
preventable cause of death in conflict-related injury, making early haemorrhage control a 
central first aid priority (International Committee of the Red Cross, 2024). 
Common injury patterns include: 
-  severe external bleeding 
-  penetrating injuries from gunshots or shrapnel 
-  blast-related polytrauma 
-  crush injuries from collapsed structures 
-  burns and inhalation injuries 
-  fractures and soft-tissue injuries  
-  minor injuries and illnesses sustained during displacement or evacuation. 
Psychological distress is also present. Exposure to violence, loss and displacement contributes to 
acute stress reactions, grief and longer-term mental health challenges for both civilians and 
responders (World Health Organization, 2013). 
Providing first aid in conflict-affected settings 
Access to first aid resources 
Access to first aid resources in conflict settings is highly unreliable and unstable. Some contexts 
may have access to trauma-focused equipment, such as tourniquets and haemostatic dressings, 
while lacking basic supplies like clean water, gloves or analgesia (pain relief). 
Supply chains are frequently disrupted by insecurity, blockades or population displacement. 
Resources may be unevenly distributed due to security priorities or power dynamics, with 
civilians often receiving delayed or inadequate access compared to armed combatants. 
Community members often rely on pre-positioned kits, improvised materials or shared 
resources, particularly in remote or besieged areas. 
In some conflict-affected settings, access to first aid and medical resources may be deliberately 
restricted or rationed based on perceived affiliation, identity or association with an opposing 
side. Civilians may be denied timely care because they are viewed as belonging to an “enemy” 
population, and individuals associated with opposition forces may face even greater barriers, 
including the intentional withholding of assistance by authorities or weapon bearers. Such 
practices are inconsistent with international humanitarian law and international human rights 
law, which require the wounded and sick to be cared for without adverse distinction. While the 
ICRC works actively to prevent and challenge these violations through dialogue, advocacy and 
presence, access to impartial care cannot always be secured in practice. 
Human resources are equally constrained. Trained healthcare workers may flee conflict zones, 
leaving volunteers and community members to provide care under extreme pressure. National 
Society volunteers are often positioned in affected communities, sharing the same risks and 
losses as those they assist. 

56
|

 
Access to advanced care 
Access to advanced care in conflict settings is unpredictable and often delayed. Health facilities 
may be damaged, overwhelmed or deliberately targeted, despite international humanitarian 
law protections (ICRC, 2016). 
Evacuation times vary widely: 
-  In some urban contexts, stabilization facilities may be nearby but unsafe to reach. 
-  In rural or remote areas, evacuation may take many hours or days. 
-  In isolated or besieged settings, evacuation may be impossible for extended periods. 
These realities require first aid systems to prepare for prolonged care, including monitoring, 
prevention of deterioration and ethical decision-making when resources are limited. As a result, 
first aid education and planning in conflict settings must assume prolonged care as a baseline 
scenario rather than an exception. 
Security and risk management 
Security considerations fundamentally shape the delivery of first aid in conflict. Responders 
must continuously assess whether it is safe to approach, treat or evacuate a casualty. Time on 
scene is often deliberately minimized to reduce exposure to danger. 
Local responders may demonstrate high risk tolerance, motivated by community ties and moral 
obligation. Over time, this can lead to the normalization of danger and cumulative psychological 
strain. International responders may operate under more restrictive security policies, which can 
limit the delivery of care. Effective systems acknowledge and manage this tension rather than 
ignore it. 
Clinical priorities 
Given injury patterns and evacuation delays, clinical priorities in conflict settings emphasize: 
-  rapid control of life-threatening bleeding, including use of pressure dressings, wound 
packing and tourniquets 
-  pelvic stabilization, often using improvised methods 
-  basic airway and breathing support consistent with trauma priorities 
-  prevention of hypothermia and shock. 
Care is often delivered in harsh environments, requiring adaptability and sound clinical 
judgment rather than rigid adherence to protocols designed for stable settings. 
First aid education in conflict-affected settings 
Educational priorities 
First aid education in conflict must prepare learners to make decisions under threat, not just to 
execute technical skills. Training should emphasize: 
-  dynamic risk assessment 
-  when to provide care and when to withdraw 
-  adaptation of techniques to security constraints (e.g. the misuse of tourniquets 
(International Committee of the Red Cross, 2024) 

|
57 

 
-  ethical considerations, including impartiality and self-protection. 
Improper or unsafe application of interventions, particularly tourniquets, has been documented 
in conflict settings and must be addressed through repeated, corrective practice (ICRC, 2018). 
Training modalities 
Experiential learning and simulation are particularly effective in this context. High-quality 
training can be delivered using low-cost materials if scenarios reflect real conditions. Key 
elements include: 
-  deliberate practice with feedback 
-  scenario-based training with increasing complexity 
-  structured debriefing to reinforce learning and address emotional impact. 
Facilitators should consider participants' fatigue, stress and nutritional needs and adjust the 
training pace appropriately. In many contexts, training periods also serve as rare opportunities 
for rest and psychological recovery. 
Learning materials and continuity 
Access to digital learning is often limited by connectivity and security. Offline materials, printed 
handouts and portable reference tools remain essential. The ICRC and National Societies have 
developed multilingual, context-adapted materials to support continuous learning when formal 
training is disrupted. 
Psychosocial and ethical considerations 
First aid providers in conflict settings are frequently members of affected communities. They 
may experience cumulative exposure to death, injury and moral dilemmas, including situations 
where care cannot be provided safely or equitably. 
Psychological first aid principles, such as ensuring safety, listening without pressure and linking 
to available support, are relevant not only for civilians but also for responders themselves 
(International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, 2015; International Federation 
of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, 2019). Peer support, informal debriefing and 
recognition of emotional burden are critical to sustaining responder capacity. 
Ethical challenges are also inherent to conflict response. Decisions about prioritization, 
withdrawal, and self-protection must be acknowledged explicitly in training rather than left 
unspoken. 
Coordination and humanitarian actors 
National Societies typically operate in close coordination with the ICRC in conflict settings, 
benefiting from shared guidance, technical support and protection mandates. Other 
humanitarian actors, local authorities and community leaders also play critical roles. 
Military medical services may be present, but coordination with civilian humanitarian actors 
requires careful navigation to preserve neutrality and trust. 

58
|

 
Conclusion 
First aid in conflict-affected settings is shaped by violence, uncertainty and moral complexity. 
The frequency of severe trauma, prolonged delays to advanced care and risks to responders 
demand a model of first aid that is adaptable, security-aware and ethically grounded. 
Education and preparedness must reflect these realities, equipping responders with not only 
technical skills but also judgment, restraint and resilience. When appropriately supported, local 
responders and communities demonstrate remarkable capacity to save lives under extreme 
conditions. 
For the Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, strengthening first aid in conflict settings is 
inseparable from the broader humanitarian commitment to protect life, dignity and access to 
care. 
 

|
59 

 
Migration 
Situational context 
Migration is an increasingly defining feature of the modern world. Every year, millions of people 
leave their homes in search of safety, reuniting with family, livelihood or better opportunities. For 
many, this journey involves navigating dangerous routes, insecure living conditions and barriers 
to healthcare and basic services. These realities make access to first aid—and the ability to 
deliver or receive it—an essential humanitarian need. 
Within the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, first aid in migration contexts 
serves not only as an emergency response but also as a means to promote dignity, trust and 
inclusion. This approach aligns with the Migration Strategy for the International Red Cross and 
Red Crescent Movement, which positions migration as a long-term humanitarian priority and 
emphasizes dignity, access to services and community-based responses across all stages of the 
migration journey (IFRC, 2025).Whether at borders, in transit zones, detention centres or urban 
neighbourhoods, the capacity to deliver timely, culturally appropriate care saves lives and 
strengthens community togetherness. 
Migrants include asylum seekers, refugees, people displaced by conflict or disasters, 
undocumented workers and individuals moving voluntarily for economic reasons. This diversity 
shapes the health challenges they face and the ways first aid must be adapted. Across the 
urban–remote continuum, first aid providers experience different logistical, cultural and ethical 
complexities, but the humanitarian principles of neutrality, impartiality and humanity remain 
constant (IFRC, 2025). 
Understanding the migration context 
While moving can create opportunity and safety, it also exposes people to injury, violence and 
environmental hazards. During transit, migrants may experience dehydration, hypothermia, 
malnutrition and exhaustion. At borders or in detention, they may face overcrowding and 
limited sanitation; in destination countries, they may endure unsafe working conditions and 
psychological stress linked to exclusion or uncertainty. 
The relationship between migration and health is complicated (IFRC, 2025). Some migrants 
experience improved health through safety and access to care, while others suffer more due to 
exploitation, stigma or interrupted treatment. Structural barriers, such as legal status, poverty, 
language and discrimination often increase these risks (IFRC & Red Cross Red Crescent Global 
Migration Lab, 2021). 
Urban settings 
Urban areas attract large numbers of migrants seeking work or refuge, but may also reinforce 
inequality. Migrants often live in overcrowded housing or informal settlements, where fire, injury 
and communicable disease risks are high. For example, during the COVID-19 pandemic, many 
migrants in cities like Kuala Lumpur and Berlin were excluded from national vaccination and 
health information systems, leading to preventable illness (IFRC & Global Migration Lab, 2021). 

60
|

 
People may technically have access to emergency care, but fear of detection or high costs may 
prevent them from using it. Language barriers and unfamiliar bureaucratic systems often 
discourage many from seeking help. For undocumented workers in construction or domestic 
labour, workplace injuries can go unreported or untreated due to fear of deportation (IFRC, 
2017). 
Urban first aid programmes must include advocacy and trust building, in addition to technical 
care, and offer safe, confidential spaces such as Humanitarian Service Points (HSPs) where 
migrants can receive assistance without discrimination. 
Remote and transit settings 
Along migration routes through deserts, mountains or seas, first aid can mean the difference 
between life and death. Remote settings are marked by limited infrastructure and supplies, and 
delayed access to advanced care. Migrants crossing the Sahara, the Mediterranean or the Darién 
Gap often face dehydration, exposure or trauma injuries without nearby health services. 
In these areas, peer-to-peer first aid frequently becomes the only available response. National 
Societies operating along major migration corridors, such as the Nigerian Red Cross Society, 
Mauritanian Red Crescent and Mexican Red Cross, train community volunteers, including 
migrants themselves, to manage common conditions including heat exhaustion, wounds and 
dehydration. These initiatives demonstrate that empowering migrants as first aid providers 
enhances both survival and solidarity (IFRC, 2025). 
Remote and mobile outreach teams must also plan for communication and referral chains 
when advanced care is hours or days away. The absence of ambulances or legal crossing 
permissions may require coordination with local authorities or humanitarian corridors to 
transport severely ill or injured individuals. 
Access to first aid and advanced care 
Migrants’ access to first aid is often inconsistent and informal. In camps or settlements, there 
might not be enough trained responders, and supplies such as bandages, gloves and 
disinfectants may be limited. Migrant associations or informal networks often serve as the initial 
point of contact, sharing information by word of mouth about where to find assistance. 
Access to advanced care, including hospitals and physicians, is even more challenging. Legal 
status, documentation and cost remain primary barriers. Asylum seekers awaiting status 
recognition may not be allowed access to public healthcare; undocumented migrants may 
avoid hospitals altogether for fear of detention or deportation (IFRC, 2016). Even when services 
are available, language and lack of digital access can make it hard to navigate complex health 
systems. 
These barriers lead to delayed or missed treatment, turning minor injuries into chronic or 
life-threatening conditions. For example, in the German Red Cross study Unseen?! Refugees 
with Disabilities in Germany, 2023, many respondents reported deterioration of existing 
conditions because they could not access rehabilitation services (German Red Cross, 2023). 
Addressing these gaps requires not only direct service delivery but trust-building and 
confidentiality guarantees so migrants know that seeking first aid will not expose them to risk. 

|
61 

 
Providing first aid in migration contexts 
Key considerations 
Providing first aid to migrants in vulnerable situations requires sensitivity to cultural, linguistic 
and legal realities. Providers must act impartially and maintain confidentiality, making sure 
there will be no legal consequences for the people to whom they provide care. Interpreters or 
cultural mediators are critical for communication, though family members should not be used 
to translate sensitive information. 
First aid providers should also be aware of trauma exposure; many migrants have experienced 
violence, loss or perilous journeys. Psychological First Aid (PFA) techniques—active listening, 
empathy and reassurance—should be used with physical care. 
Where trust is low, visibility and neutrality matter. Distinct Red Cross and Red Crescent emblems 
help migrants identify safe assistance points. Field teams must coordinate with protection and 
legal services when they suspect abuse or exploitation. 
Common health and injury patterns 
Migrants face injuries and illnesses linked to their environment and livelihoods: 
-  During transit – dehydration, hypothermia, heatstroke, exhaustion, cuts and grazes 
wounds, and fractures, sprains, and strains from walking long distances. 
-  At sea – hypothermia, saltwater sores, drowning risk and trauma from overcrowded 
vessels. 
-  In camps or shelters – respiratory infections, gastrointestinal illness, scabies and minor 
burns from unsafe cooking areas. 
-  At work – falls, crush injuries, chemical exposure and repetitive strain injuries. 
-  Psychological distress – anxiety, insomnia, post-traumatic symptoms or grief. 
First aid programmes should therefore combine basic physical interventions with psychosocial 
care and referral pathways to specialized services when possible. 
Urban versus remote care considerations 
In urban areas, first aid provision focuses on outreach and inclusion. Mobile units or fixed HSPs in 
transport hubs and city outskirts provide immediate aid, distribute hygiene kits and connect 
migrants to clinics. Coordination with municipal authorities helps provide continued care while 
maintaining neutrality.   
In remote areas, survival is the priority. Volunteers may operate with minimal supplies, 
improvising splints, pressure dressings and shelter. Communication equipment and referral 
partnerships are vital. When advanced care is delayed, monitoring, documentation and 
prevention of infection or dehydration become central responsibilities. 
Both contexts highlight the need for context-specific training and adaptable equipment. Light, 
portable first aid kits and multilingual guidance cards enhance efficiency and accessibility. 

62
|

 
First aid education for and with migrants 
Training migrants as first aid providers 
Empowering migrants through first aid education supports independence, safety and 
community resilience. Training should be accessible, relevant and trauma-informed. Courses 
must respect language diversity and literacy levels using visual materials, videos or 
demonstrations instead of text-heavy manuals. 
For migrants on the move, training sessions should be short, flexible and location-responsive, 
delivered in transit centres or temporary shelters. Portable materials, such as laminated cards or 
mobile apps, allow learners to refresh their skills after relocation. In urban or stable contexts, 
multi-day courses can provide comprehensive instruction on both physical and psychological 
first aid. 
Training should focus on practical scenarios that migrants are most likely to face: dehydration, 
burns, musculoskeletal injuries, fainting and stress reactions. Incorporating peer-to-peer 
learning reinforces trust and cultural relevance. 
Training staff and volunteers supporting migrants 
For Red Cross and Red Crescent staff and volunteers, cultural competence and trauma 
awareness are essential. Trainers should use participatory methods and facilitate discussion on 
ethical dilemmas, confidentiality and safe referral. Sessions must emphasize that first aid 
providers are humanitarian actors, not extensions of state authorities, to create a sense of safety 
and trust with migrants. 
Interpreters and cultural mediators should be integrated into the planning and delivery process. 
Scenario-based exercises can model sensitive communication, helping participants avoid 
unintentional triggers. Continuous supervision, feedback and refresher training maintain quality 
and confidence (IFRC, 2017). 
Psychological first aid and empowerment 
Psychological First Aid should be a standard module in all migration-related programmes. It 
equips responders to manage distress compassionately and empowers migrants to support one 
another. Learning environments must be psychologically safe (avoiding role plays that replicate 
traumatic events) and should encourage reflection on hope, coping and community strengths. 
Education modalities and accessibility 
First aid education in migration contexts must reflect mobility and diversity. Effective modalities 
include: 
-  Modular learning: brief, stand-alone sessions adaptable to transit or camp settings. 
-  Visual instruction: diagrams, animations and video translation for multilingual audiences.

title: Severe bleeding control (tourniquets, packing, pressure)
text:
254
|

 
 
 
 
 
 
TRAUMA 
 
 

FIRST AID
|
255 

 
Severe bleeding 
Key action 
Apply direct pressure to the area to control the bleeding as quickly as possible.  
Introduction 
Severe external bleeding is a life-threatening condition requiring urgent first aid. The human 
body relies on blood circulating around the body to deliver oxygen and glucose to organs and 
tissues such as the heart, brain and skin. If a person loses a lot of blood, their circulatory system 
may fail and be unable to deliver enough oxygen to their body. This can lead to shock and, 
ultimately, death if not addressed. Common causes of life-threatening bleeding include road 
traffic collisions, machinery accidents, knife wounds and gunshot injuries. External bleeding 
forms the basis of this topic. See also Chest and abdomen injuries and Amputation for 
information on treating those types of injuries. 
Internal bleeding, such as unseen bleeding into the chest or abdominal cavity, is also 
life-threatening. Management of internal bleeding is outlined in Shock, with emphasis on 
recognition and positioning. 
Guidelines 
-  First aid providers should use direct manual compression for life-threatening external 
bleeding.** 
-  First aid providers should not use pressure points (indirect manual pressure) or ice to stop 
bleeding.** 
-  If direct manual compression is ineffective or unable to be performed, first aid providers 
may use a tourniquet for severe, life-threatening external extremity bleeding.* 
-  If a tourniquet is used, a manufactured tourniquet is preferred. An improvised tourniquet 
may be less effective than a manufactured tourniquet, but may be applied if that is all 
that is available for severe, life-threatening external extremity bleeding.* 
-  First aid providers may use a manufactured windlass tourniquet for the management of 
life-threatening extremity bleeding in children.* 
-  If direct manual compression is ineffective, and a tourniquet is not practical, available or 
appropriate, a haemostatic dressing may be used for severe, life-threatening external 
bleeding. The haemostatic dressing should be applied directly to the source of bleeding 
with direct pressure.* 
Good practice points 
-  Emergency medical services (EMS) should be accessed for all severe bleeding. 
-  First aid providers should protect themselves from the person’s blood by putting on 
gloves or covering their hands (e.g. with plastic bags, bandages or clothing).  
-  First aid providers (or the injured person, if able) should apply direct manual compression 
rather than applying a bandage that wraps around the body part to apply even pressure 

256
|

 
(also called a circumferential pressure dressing) to a severe bleed. If bandages are 
available, they can be used to apply pressure. Once severe bleeding has been controlled, a 
bandage may be applied to the wound. However, if a bandage is unavailable, clean 
materials such as clothes or towels may be used as improvised bandages. 
-  If the bleeding cannot be stopped, first aid providers should consider: 
○ applying consistent, direct pressure with more force  
○ applying a tourniquet to an extremity wound and ensuring it is sufficiently 
tightened 
○ applying a haemostatic dressing on the wound while continuing to apply direct 
pressure. 
-  First aid providers should apply pressure around an embedded object (e.g. a knife) to 
stabilize the object. Avoid removing the object. 
-  Tourniquets should only be used for life-threatening extremity (i.e. limb) bleeding. They 
may help save a life, but may have severe consequences (e.g. amputation of the limb), 
especially if applied for too long. Once a tourniquet has been applied, keep it in place until 
EMS arrive. 
Chain of survival behaviours 
Prevent and prepare 
-  Learn how to control bleeding using the resources likely to be available, such as 
bandages, clothing or manufactured tourniquets. 
Early recognition 
-  Blood is flowing or spurting from a wound. 
-  Action to stem the flow of blood should be taken as soon as possible. Even a cupful of 
blood, although not immediately life-threatening, can lead to fast deterioration if not 
stopped early on. 
First aid steps 
1.
Ask the person to apply direct pressure to their injury with their hands. 
2. Help the person to lie down. 
3. Access EMS. 
4. Apply direct pressure to the bleed. If blood soaks through the dressing, apply a second 
dressing over the first one and apply greater pressure. 
5. If direct pressure is ineffective and the person is bleeding from an arm or leg, consider 
applying a tourniquet or haemostatic dressing, if available. Continue to put direct 
pressure on the bleed. In the case that a tourniquet is ineffective, you can add a second 
tourniquet above the first. 
6. Shock is likely to develop from significant bleeding. Help the person into a comfortable 
position and keep them warm by wrapping them in clothing or blankets if necessary. 
 
If the injured person can apply pressure to their own wound, this can reduce the risk of 
cross-infection and keep both the first aid provider and the injured person safe. 

FIRST AID
|
257 

 
If the injured person becomes unresponsive, open their airway and check for breathing after 
stopping the bleeding. 
 
 
SPECIAL CASES 
-  In situations of disaster or conflict, including war, terror attack or violent attack (such as 
shooting or stabbing), the safety and security of the first aid provider and the injured person 
are paramount and take precedence over providing immediate care.  
-  The application of tourniquets in these situations may be used as the first short-term “stop 
the bleed” measure, to either deal with the overwhelming number of injured people or to 
get people with severe life-threatening bleeding out of an immediate danger zone. In both 
cases, the release of the tourniquet should only be considered under the guidance of a 
medical professional. 
Access help 
-  Severe bleeding is a life-threatening condition requiring medical care. Clearly explain the 
cause of the injury and the condition of the person to EMS so they can prioritize your case 
accurately. 
Education considerations 
Context considerations 
-  Consider the local health system, especially the availability of well-developed emergency 
care and manufactured tourniquets, to decide whether to include tourniquet education. 
-  Consider local laws and regulations, as well as the availability of haemostatic dressings, 
before including them in learning design. 
-  Some contexts may have a high incidence of bloodborne pathogens (e.g. HIV), or there 
may be a low incidence but high levels of fear about them. In these contexts, allow 
learners to consider real versus perceived risks associated with the transmission, and 
reinforce good universal precautions. 
-  Use scenarios built around the local industry (e.g. agriculture) or local factors such as road 
traffic behaviour, violent conflict or crime, to make education on this topic relevant to 
learners. 
Learner considerations 
-  Consider where learners live and work and discuss the most likely causes of injuries that 
cause bleeding in the local setting to give context and relevance to the topic. 
-  This topic can be quite graphic (both in training and in reality). The use of images and 
video can be helpful in preparing learners for what they might see in reality. However, this 
may be unsuitable for children and some other learner groups. Scenarios and storytelling 
with or without actors might produce engagement without fear and upset. 
-  Conversely, the use of fake blood to create scenarios and pretend injuries can be 
fascinating and informative for learners and encourage engagement. 

258
|

 
-  Check whether learners have a first aid kit, dressings or manufactured tourniquets in their 
homes, or whether they might be able to access them (Andrade et al., 2020). 
-  Consider only including haemostatic dressings in training for more advanced first aid 
providers and in instances where learners may enter remote areas. 
Facilitation tips 
-  Discuss with learners how to recognize a severe bleed: how much blood is coming out? 
What does it look like? Discuss it in terms of volume (e.g. cup-full, ounces); how it looks 
(forming a puddle or pool, soaking through the bandage) and the emotional reaction 
they might have (Pellegrino et al., 2020). 
-  Emphasize that timely intervention to stop bleeding is vital and may be a life-saving 
action. Applying pressure to a bleed is often a simple action, easy to do and can be very 
effective. 
-  Support learners to practise feeling how much and what sort of pressure is needed to 
stop a bleed and how this will feel for the injured person. Consider different postures that 
learners could take to apply sufficient pressure depending on their physical strength 
(Charlton et al., 2019). 
-  Discuss with learners what they should do depending on where the bleed is coming from 
on the body: when to use a tourniquet (on a limb) or when to apply pressure or use a 
dressing (Pellegrino et al., 2020). 
-  Discuss the practicalities of there being a lot of blood and what to do when a bandage is 
soaked through. Explain that the pressure will be reduced if more and more bandages 
are applied (Charlton et al., 2018). 
-  Encourage learners to think creatively about the materials they have nearby in their 
relevant contexts that could be used to stop a bleed, such as a clean towel or T-shirt. 
Emphasize that even if there is nothing available, they can apply pressure with their own 
hand if they do not have any open cuts, as the risk of infection is very low. 
-  Emphasize the importance of direct pressure before finding a bandage to apply. Once 
the flow of blood has been stopped using pressure, help learners to practise applying a 
bandage so that it is secure and maintains sufficient pressure. Try bandaging different 
body parts. 
-  The topic of bleeding has many potential barriers that could reduce learners’ intention to 
help, such as infection, fear of blood or concerns of violence. While these should be 
explored, the aim should be to develop pro-helping strategies. 
-  Explore ways learners can protect themselves and the injured person from blood-borne 
viruses while still providing life-saving care if this is a concern (e.g. they could wear gloves 
or ask the injured person who is bleeding to apply pressure to their own wound). Avoid 
creating a barrier to helping through fear of infection. Explore what alternatives may be 
available if a person does not have gloves (e.g. a plastic bag). 
-  Facilitate a discussion on the common fear of blood, highlighting it as a potential barrier 
to providing help. Allow learners to practise dealing with bleeding if it may help build their 
confidence or develop other strategies to overcome their barriers (e.g. directing the 
injured person to apply pressure to their own wound). 
-  Emphasize that objects embedded in a wound should be left where they are if there is 
the possibility of severe bleeding, as the object may be acting as a “plug”. Removing it 
may make the bleeding worse. 

FIRST AID
|
259 

 
Tourniquets and haemostatic dressings 
-  If teaching learners about tourniquets, train them on how and when to use them for safe 
and effective use. Tourniquets are powerful tools for bleeding control but can also cause 
harm if used incorrectly. Emphasize that tourniquets should only be used when direct 
pressure on the bleed is ineffective and the injury is on a limb. 
-  Consider what style of tourniquet is available locally and train in that specific style. 
Training in applying one style of a tourniquet will not necessarily facilitate skill transfer to 
other tourniquet styles (McCarty et al., 2019). 
-  Discuss why improvised tourniquets might be less effective. This could be because they 
cannot be adequately tightened to provide the required amount of pressure and are 
more likely to break  (McCarty et al., 2019). 
-  Emphasize that the application of a tourniquet is very painful if done correctly, and the 
injured person may respond violently and try to remove the tourniquet. By being 
prepared for this the first aid provider can ensure their own safety, but also prepare the 
injured person, which will make it easier for them to cope with the pain. 
-  If haemostatic dressings are included in education, training in the proper assessment of 
severe bleeding and the dressing application techniques are required. Emphasize they 
should only be used in instances of life-threatening bleeding (Goolsby et al., 2019; Zietlow 
et al., 2015). 
Facilitation tools 
-  Provide a glossary of words or phrases that may be used interchangeably (e.g. bleeding 
and haemorrhage). 
-  Discussing what “severe bleeding” means and looks like could be a useful starter for this 
topic. This could take place as a discussion exercise using a flipchart with the heading, 
“What other words can you think of that describe ‘severe bleeding’?” Answers may 
include gushing, flowing, spouting, running like an open tap, soaking through the 
bandage or pooling on the floor. 
○ This could be followed by exercises using images and the questions: 
■ What do you think has happened here? 
■ How badly is this person bleeding? 
■ What happens when someone loses a lot of blood? 
■ How do they look? 
■ How do you think they might be feeling or might behave? 
■ What do you think will happen next? 
○ Facilitators can use this to develop a “common language” and understanding for 
the rest of the topic. 
-  Encourage learners to share their experiences with severe bleeding, and ask groups to 
explore the topic through storytelling and role play scenarios. Role play can be particularly 
beneficial as a dynamic and interactive learning format. 
-  It may be useful to show how different clothing or flooring can affect the perception of 
how much blood has been lost. Soil or thick clothing, for example, can demonstrate how 
severe blood loss can be hidden. 
-  Use a range of objects to demonstrate bleeding and how to treat it. For example, get a 
plastic bottle (full of water coloured with food dye). This could be wrapped up in clothing

Chest and abdomen injuries 
Key action 
Help the person to lie down in a comfortable position, contact emergency services and monitor 
the person closely. 
Introduction 
A chest injury includes any injury to the ribs, heart and lungs, while an abdominal wound 
includes any injury to the abdomen (may be an injury of the organs, not necessarily). Some chest 
wounds are “open”, which means there is a hole in the chest, usually caused by injuries such as a 
gunshot or stabbing. It is also possible to have sucking or blowing chest wounds, which can 
cause severe breathing difficulties. Learners should recognize open chest and abdominal 
wounds as potentially life-threatening and be able to provide care. 
Guidelines 
-  First aid providers should not use an occlusive dressing on a person with an open chest 
wound.* 
Good practice points 
-  Safety and security are paramount, and in situations of danger, first aid providers need to 
be alert to the risks they face from weapons and aggression. 
-  First aid providers should consider the potential for blunt force trauma in the event of a 
gunshot, blast or knife injury to someone wearing a ballistic vest. 
-  First aid providers should help a person with a chest or abdominal injury to lie down in a 
comfortable position. For someone with a chest injury, this may be lying semi-propped up 
on their affected side. For someone with an abdominal injury, this may be lying down 
with bent legs. 
-  If there is significant external bleeding from an abdominal wound, direct pressure with or 
without a haemostatic dressing should be applied.  
-  An open chest wound that is not actively bleeding may be left open, without the 
application of a dressing, because a sealed wound may allow air to build up in the chest, 
which may lead to the lung partially or fully collapsing (pneumothorax). 
-  If applying pressure to an open chest wound, ensure the pressure does not completely 
seal the wound. If the wound is bubbling or making noise, do not completely seal the 
wound. 
-  If a dressing is necessary on an open chest wound (e.g. to transport the person a long 
distance to receive medical care), a non-occlusive dressing may be used. 
-  A sterile (or functionally clean) and wet dressing may be placed on open abdominal 
wounds where internal organs are visible. 
-  First aid providers should not push internal organs back into the body. 
-  Impaled objects in the body should be stabilized, and if the object is pulsating, it should 
be allowed to do so while loosely stabilized. 

FIRST AID
|
267 

 
-  First aid providers should access emergency medical care for all penetrating chest or 
abdominal wounds. 
-  First aid providers should treat the person for Shock. This may include helping the person 
to lie down in a comfortable position and keeping them warm. 
Chain of survival behaviours 
Prevent and prepare 
-  In workplaces where there is a high risk of falls, crush injuries or explosion risks, such as 
construction and mining, include training on this topic and provide appropriate first aid 
equipment. 
-  Wear a ballistic vest when entering a conflict zone if possible. 
Early recognition 
The person has experienced physical trauma, such as from a road traffic collision, a weapon or a 
fall. You may not be able to see the wound as it might be internal or under clothing. Talk to the 
person and ask them about their condition to locate the injury as quickly as possible. There may 
be multiple wounds from a single projectile. 
A person who has experienced physical trauma may have an internal injury that is bleeding 
inside their chest or abdomen. This may only become apparent if the person starts to show 
signs of shock. 
A person with an open chest wound may have difficult or painful breathing, and they may 
cough up blood. 
First aid steps 
Once in a safe location, examine the person as carefully and thoroughly as possible.

Other roles in providing medical care 
There are other roles that provide medical care. These are often referred to collectively as 
advanced care. They include: 
First responder 
-  A first responder has a professional responsibility to respond as a primary role of their 
position. 
-  First responders are often dispatched by a central organization and are directed to the 
incident; they are typically the first step in a formal emergency medical service. 
Paramedic 
-  A paramedic provides advanced care according to their profession in varied 
environments. 
-  A paramedic may be the first responder to arrive in an emergency.  
-  A paramedic can often provide sufficient care for the person to return to their activities; 
however, a paramedic also provides transport services to other health services as required 
(e.g. hospital). 
In-hospital care 
-  In-hospital care refers to the services provided by doctors, nurses and other healthcare 
professionals who deliver emergency care within the hospital setting. Those providing 
in-hospital care work in a controlled environment with access to all required tools and 
professionals available.

Using the Guidelines 2025 
Because this document is extensive, it is encouraged to use its built-in navigation features to 
move efficiently between sections.  
-  Key topics are linked throughout the guidelines to help readers make connections across 
content; for example, CPR is generally linked to the topic on unresponsiveness and 
abnormal breathing for adults and adolescents, with a clear cross-link to the child and 
baby topic.  
-  An easy-to-access table of contents on the inside cover allows quick navigation to 
guideline chapters. 
-  The topic index offers a more comprehensive way to locate specific subjects across 
contexts and populations.  
-  The gear icon ( ⚙️) at the bottom of even-numbered pages provides direct access to the 
topic index from anywhere in the document.  
-  Referencing is integrated through in-text citations in parentheses throughout, with a 
consolidated reference list at the end of the document, organized into four sections for 
ease of use: Contextualizing first aid and first aid education, First aid education, First aid 
and Resuscitation. 
Future development 
These Guidelines are not exhaustive. For this edition, topics requested by National Societies and 
others considered current and relevant have been included. First aid topics that were not 
reviewed have been excluded from this list. National Societies are invited to reach out to the 
Global First Aid Reference Centre if there are topics for which they need an evidence base to be 
considered for future analysis. 
 

INTRODUCTION
|
19 

 
Process to develop the 2025 Guidelines 
Red Cross and Red Crescent National Societies independently developed their national 
guidelines for many years. Since 2011, the IFRC, through the Global First Aid Reference Centre, 
has published evidence-based international guidelines drawing on the best available science 
and practices from the field. 
In 2022, following the successful adoption of First Aid Vision 2030 at the General Assembly, the 
Global First Aid Reference Centre began the process of updating and developing the 

recruiting subject matter experts and conducting a needs analysis with first aid education 
programme developers to determine priority topics. The Steering Committee established a 
structured process for conducting evidence reviews and cataloguing evidence-based practices. 
Evidence-based guidelines 
Approach to the development of evidence-based guidelines 
The Guidelines are developed in accordance with the principles of evidence-based practice. 
Evidence-based guidelines integrate three key sources of information: 
1.
The best available scientific evidence, identified and collected through systematic 
database searches. 
2. Practical experience and expertise contributed by experts in the field. 
3. Preferences, values and available resources of target groups, such as first aid providers 
and people receiving first aid, to ensure recommendations are relevant and feasible. 
The Steering Committee began by selecting the topics to be included in the Guidelines. In 
addition to the existing topics, one new topic, anxiety and panic, was identified for inclusion. For 
each topic, the Committee systematically collected up-to-date evidence. 
As a leader in first aid, resuscitation and education science, the IFRC network has traditionally 
worked in partnership with local resuscitation councils and their parent organizations. In 2024, 
the IFRC became an official Collaborating Member with the International Liaison Committee on 
Resuscitation (ILCOR) and formally contributed to the Consensus on Science and Treatment 
Recommendations. For the 2025 Guidelines, ILCOR publications from 2020 to 2025 were 
consulted for topics relevant to the IFRC. In addition, evidence summaries developed by the 
Centre for Evidence-Based Practice of the Belgian Red Cross–Flanders were updated between 
2023 and 2025. 
Where an evidence summary was considered stable, meaning the evidence was of high 
certainty or the intervention was widely accepted as common sense and supported by existing 
evidence, no further updates were undertaken. 
Education topics followed a similar development process. With input from first aid educators 
and the Steering Committee, the list of education topics was revised by consolidating previous 
topics and developing new ones to respond to the needs of first aid educators across the 
International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement. Evidence summaries were updated 
through a systematic review process. A total of 5,295 manuscripts identified through systematic 

20
|

 
searches related to first aid and first aid education were sorted by topic. Two to three first aid 
education experts from diverse global regions synthesized the relevant studies to inform the 
updated Guidelines. 
Based on the updated evidence, draft recommendations were revised as needed. Monthly 
conference calls were held to monitor progress. Each topic was developed collaboratively by 
members of the clinical and education working groups. 
Clinical topics were reviewed by the clinical working group, after which educational 
considerations were added through a review of education-focused literature and expert input. 
Topics were framed using the chain of survival behaviours. Reviewers with expertise from both 
high- and low-resource settings were consulted. For topics particularly relevant to conflict 
settings, reviewers from the ICRC provided expert input and additional literature insights. ILCOR 
members also reviewed topics aligned with ILCOR publications to ensure consistency. 
Engagement and contextualization 
In spring 2025, an Engagement Committee was established to support the contextualization of 
the Guidelines. This committee included 66 participants from all five IFRC Regions–Africa, 
Americas, Asia-Pacific, Europe and Middle East-North Africa–and met eight times over three 
months to review 24 topics. More than 500 recommendations were considered for inclusion. 
Recommendations were incorporated into education considerations and chain of survival 
behaviours to support local implementation. 
Use of generative artificial intelligence 
ChatGPT (GPT-5) was used as a language-support tool to promote consistency and clarity 
throughout the document. It supported synthesis of contributions from multiple volunteer 
authors and organizations and alignment of terminology. The use of generative AI reflects 
emerging, accepted practices in the humanitarian sector to responsibly apply digital tools that 
enhance collaboration, inclusivity and efficiency, while maintaining human oversight, 
transparency and ethical standards. All content refined using generative AI was reviewed, edited 
and verified by human authors to ensure accuracy, clarity and fidelity to the intended meaning. 
Generative AI was used specifically to support the development of the 2025 Guidelines front 
matter, Evidence to action, Contexts and Education sections. 
Structure of the Guidelines 
Significant effort was made to clearly link recommendations to first aid education. Each topic 
now includes expanded content to support programme designers in developing confident and 
capable first aid providers. Education is emphasized as the primary mechanism for building 
ability and confidence, reflected in the inclusion of education in the Guidelines title.  
Each topic includes: 
-  Key action 
-  Introduction

title: Fractures, crush injury and immobilization
text:
Facilitation tips 
-  Establish what learners already know about how to treat burns and uncover any strong 
beliefs. This information will help identify any knowledge gaps as well as any 
non-evidence-based practices or misconceptions (e.g. putting butter or cooking oil on a 
burn). 
-  Emphasize that cooling the burn is critical to reducing any potential tissue damage. The 
burning effect continues even after the skin has been removed from the source of heat so 
cooling should take place quickly and for a sustained time (10 minutes minimum). 
-  Explore how burns look on different skin types and colours. 
-  Provide learners with time to practise making the person comfortable while cooling their 
burn. While the recommended time to cool a burn is specific, this may present a 
challenge if the person does not want to cooperate. Children, in particular, find it hard to 
sit still and the cold water can start to cause them pain. 
Facilitation tools 
-  In 2017, the Belgian Red Cross-Flanders updated the manual Basic First Aid for Africa 
(revised in 2016), which has some interesting material on prevention and when to seek 
medical help regarding burns (Belgian Red Cross-Flanders, 2017). 

292
|

 
Learning connections 
-  Hypothermia and shock are both conditions that might develop following a burn. 
Scientific foundation 
Systematic reviews 
The scientific foundation for this section is based on a 2015 evidence review and 2020 scoping 
review from the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) First Aid Task Force, 
evidence summaries from the Centre of Evidence-Based Practice (CEBaP, 2019; CEBaP, 2020), 
and a Cochrane review. 
Cooling 
ILCOR identified one randomized controlled trial and four observational studies in a 2015 
evidence review (Singletary, et al., 2015; Zideman et al., 2015). Based on one randomized 
controlled trial and one observational study, no difference in pain could be shown in cooled 
versus non-cooled burns (low-certainty evidence). In the randomized controlled trial, a difference 
in the amount of erythema could not be shown (low-certainty evidence). Two observational 
studies showed a reduction in the depth of a burn when cooling, whereas a third observational 
study found no benefit of cooling (low- to very low-certainty evidence). In one observational 
study, no benefit in reducing re-epithelialization time was shown (very low-certainty evidence). 
Three observational studies looked at the need for medical care. Two studies showed a 
decreased length of hospital stay after a minimum of 10 minutes of cooling, and a decrease in 
hospital admission after a media campaign about the cooling of burns, whereas the third study 
showed no difference (very low-certainty evidence). In addition, in 2021 ILCOR published a 
systematic review about the optimal duration of cooling (Wyckoff et al., 2021; Wyckoff et al., 
2022a; Djärv et al., 2022) and identified four observational studies. For the outcome of burn size, 
no significant difference was shown when cooling a burn for 20 minutes compared with cooling 
for less than 20 minutes (very low-certainty evidence). When it comes to the degree of the burn, 
inconsistent evidence was found. ILCOR concluded that a specific duration of cooling cannot be 
recommended at this time. 
Ice 
A Centre of Evidence-Based Practice (CEBaP) evidence summary revealed there is limited 
evidence from one observational study, either in favour of using ice or of no treatment. A 
statistically significant decrease in the need for grafts, scar management, days to re-epithelialize 
or the number of visits, using ice compared to no treatment, could not be demonstrated. 
Evidence is of very low certainty and results cannot be considered precise due to a low number 
of events, limited sample size and large variability of results. The updated evidence summary did 
not identify any new studies. 
Deroofing 
A CEBaP evidence summary shows that there is limited evidence from one non-randomized 
controlled trial in favour of keeping a blister intact (i.e. not removing the top layer of skin from 
the blister). It was shown that keeping a blister intact resulted in a statistically significant 
decrease in bacteria or Staphylococcus aureus colonization, compared to aspirating or deroofing 

FIRST AID
|
293 

 
a blister. Evidence is of low certainty and results cannot be considered precise due to limited 
sample size, the low number of events and lack of data. The updated evidence summary did not 
identify any new studies. 
Burn dressings 
A scoping review conducted by ILCOR in 2020 identified no studies on burn dressings in the first 
aid setting for superficial thermal burns (Markenson et al., 2019). Additionally, a Cochrane review 
was identified that reported on the use of dressings for superficial and partial-thickness burns 
(Wasiak et al., 2013). Silver sulfadiazine was consistently associated with poorer healing outcomes 
compared to biosynthetic (skin substitute) dressings, silver-containing dressings and 
silicon-coated dressings. It was also reported that burns treated with hydrogel dressings 
appeared to heal more quickly than those treated with usual care. The review authors concluded 
that it was impossible to draw firm and confident conclusions about the effectiveness of specific 
dressings. A follow-up systematic review by the same group (Goodwin et al., 2015) did not find 
any studies on the use of hydrogel-based burn dressings in first aid practices in the prehospital 
setting. 
Alternative burn dressings (honey, fatty acids, banana leaf dressings, vaseline) 
An updated 2024 CEBaP evidence summary includes a Cochrane systematic review and four 
additional randomized controlled trials about the use of honey to treat burns. No additional 
studies were identified during the update.  It was shown that honey resulted in a statistically 
significant decrease in the mean time to healing and incidence of infection compared to 
conventional non-antimicrobial dressings. It was also shown that honey resulted in a statistically 
significant decrease in time to complete healing, presence and completion of epithelialization, 
hospital stay, persistent infection and time until negative swabs compared to silver sulfadiazine. 
A statistically significant decrease in the mean time to healing, number of healing events, 
incident infection, clinical infections or adverse events, using honey compared to silver 
sulfadiazine, could not be demonstrated. Finally, it was shown that honey resulted in a 
statistically significant decrease in time to complete healing, mean time to healing and 
persistent infection compared to potato peelings. A statistically significant decrease in adverse 
events was not demonstrated when using honey compared to potato peelings. Evidence is of 
moderate to low certainty and results cannot be considered precise due to limited sample size, a 
low number of events, lack of data or large variability of results. 
Updated in 2024, an additional CEBaP evidence summary identified evidence about the use of 
fatty acids and banana leaf dressings as burn dressings. There is limited evidence from one 
non-randomized controlled trial in favour of fatty acids (ethyl linoleate). It was demonstrated that 
adjuvant topical application of ethyl linoleate led to a statistically significant decrease in the 
requirement for narcotic pain relief, the time to appearance of epithelium, the appearance of 
normal pigment and hair and the number of patients requiring grafts compared to standard 
burn management. A statistically significant decrease in length of hospital stay, amount of 
positive cultures, the number of patients requiring reconstructions and mortality, using adjuvant 
ethyl linoleate compared to standard burn management, could not be demonstrated. 
There is limited evidence from two non-randomized controlled trials and one cohort study in 
favour of banana leaf dressings. It was shown that banana leaf dressings resulted in a statistically 

294
|

 
significant decrease in discomfort score, dressing removal pain score, intake of pain medication 
and time to complete healing, and an increase in ease of dressing removal and satisfaction with 
dressing method, compared to using ordinary gauze dressings. In another study, it was shown 
that banana leaf dressings resulted in a statistically significant decrease in discomfort score 20 
minutes after dressing and in pain score before dressing. A statistically significant decrease in 
discomfort score before and during dressing, as well as a pain score during and after dressing, 
could not be demonstrated. A statistically significant decrease in signs of wound infection or 
length of hospital stay, using banana leaf dressings compared to ordinary gauze dressings could 
not be demonstrated. A statistically significant difference in complete epithelialization, need for 
skin grafting, dressing change pain and discomfort using banana leaf dressings compared with 
boiled potato peel dressings could not be demonstrated. All evidence is of very low certainty and 
results cannot be considered precise due to limited sample size, the large variability of results 
and lack of data. 
Another CEBaP evidence summary, updated in 2024, revealed there is limited evidence from 
one randomized controlled trial and one cohort study in favour of using vaseline. It was shown 
that 
vaseline 
application resulted in a statistically significant decrease in time to 
re-epithelialization, adherence to the wound and time to change the dressing, and a statistically 
significant increase in ease of dressing removal compared to silver sulfadiazine covered with a 
gauze. A statistically significant decrease in pain during dressing application, pain during 
dressing removal, amount of dressing changes and infection rate using vaseline compared to 
silver sulfadiazine or polysporin covered with gauze could not be demonstrated. The evidence is 
of very low certainty for the outcome of infection rate and of moderate certainty for all other 
outcomes. The results cannot be considered precise due to the limited sample size. 
Plastic cling wrap 
A 2024 CEBaP evidence summary identified one randomized controlled trial on the use of cling 
wrap or plastic film on burn wounds. A statistically significant decrease in pain and days to 
re-epithelialization could not be demonstrated when comparing plasticized polyvinylchloride 
film (clingfilm) with burnaid hydrogel. This suggests that clingfilm may be as effective as 
hydrogel dressings for the temporary coverage of burn wounds until specialized care is available. 
However, the certainty of the evidence is low, as the findings are based on a small sample size 
and show considerable variability. 
Chemical burn 
A CEBaP evidence summary showed that there is limited evidence from two observational 
studies in favour of immediate irrigation of the burned skin with tap water or diphoterine. It was 
shown that immediate irrigation with tap water resulted in a statistically significant decrease in 
length of hospital stay and number of full-thickness burns, compared to no immediate irrigation 
with tap water or irrigation with saline, isotonic phosphate buffer or Ringer’s lactate. It was also 
shown that irrigation with diphoterine resulted in a statistically significant decreased proportion 
of severe burn wounds, compared to irrigation with tap water. Evidence is of very low certainty 
and results cannot be considered precise due to low sample size, a low number of events, large 
variability in results and a lack of data. The updated evidence summary did not identify any new 
studies. 

FIRST AID
|
295 

 
A second CEBaP evidence summary revealed that there is limited evidence from three 
observational studies in favour of immediate irrigation of the burned eye with tap water or 
diphoterine. It was shown that immediate irrigation (with tap water) resulted in a statistically 
significant decrease in the proportion of severe burns, corneal and conjunctival erosion, time 
until healing less than seven days and the number of eye operations needed, and a statistically 
significant increase in clear vision and the proportion of mild eye injuries, compared to no 
immediate irrigation (with tap water) or irrigation with saline, isotonic phosphate buffer or 
Ringer’s lactate. A statistically significant difference in the proportion of severe burn wounds 
after irrigation with tap water, compared to irrigation with diphoterine, could not be 
demonstrated. Additionally, a statistically significant difference in the proportion of conjunctivitis 
or superficial punctate keratitis was not demonstrated between immediate irrigation and no 
immediate irrigation. Evidence is of very low certainty and results cannot be considered precise 
due to low sample size, a low number of events and large variability in results. The updated 
evidence summary did not identify any new studies. 
There is no evidence summary available on what to do if a chemical substance is ingested. 
Sunburn 
A 2019 evidence summary from CEBaP found limited evidence from four experimental studies 
in favour of aftersun lotion and aftersun cream, and from two experimental studies in favour of 
aftersun gel. The evidence was declared stable and the evidence summary was therefore not 
updated. 
It was shown that aftersun lotion (Hamamelis-free lotion) and aftersun cream (aloe vera cream) 
resulted in a statistically significant reduction in erythema (48–54 hours after sun exposure) 
compared to a placebo lotion or cream or no treatment. On the other hand, in two studies using 
aftersun cream (aloe vera cream), a statistical erythema reduction 24 hours after sun exposure, 
compared to placebo or no treatment, could not be demonstrated. Evidence is of low certainty 
and results cannot be considered precise due to limited sample size, the low number of events 
and a lack of data. 
It was shown that aftersun lotion with 0.1% diclofenac resulted in a statistically significant 
reduction in erythema and pain, compared to a placebo gel (Kienzler et al., 2005; Magnette et al., 
2004). 
Evidence is of moderate certainty and results cannot be considered precise due to limited 
sample size. 
Education review 
We initially sourced 13 papers through the education search strategy for this topic, of which we 
included seven. Expert reviewers added a paper, bringing the total to eight. These include the 
following: 
-  one systematic review from Nurmatov et al. (2017) 
-  two literature reviews from Bitter et al. (2016) and Forjuoh et al. (2006) 
-  one mini meta-analysis of studies from Tanzania by Outwater et al. (2018) 

296
|

 
-  four studies on knowledge and awareness from Alomar et al. (2016), Ghosh and Bharat 
(2000), Graham et al. (2011) and Wallace et al. (2013). 
Language 
Nurmatov et al. (2017) identified that awareness, knowledge and practice of burn first aid skills is 
low among caregivers worldwide; many people either do not cool the burn properly or do not 
cool it long enough. Public messaging adds to the confusion by providing a variety of 
recommendations and guidelines. This confusion was evident across the papers we reviewed 
where each had different “ideal” burn treatments. The review found that when public 
messaging appears in the local language, knowledge and behaviour change is possible. It
